hypotheses.claim: The recent code change that raised MAX_RETRIES to 10 and set BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS to 0.0 caused immediate, rapid retries, producing the outbound request surge and downstream overload.
hypotheses.supporting_reasoning: The diff shows the retry ceiling was increased from 2 to 10 and any back‑off delay was removed. The loop in EV-CODE-003 will now iterate up to ten times without pause. Logs EV-LOG-004‑006 record three immediate retries for the same charge within the same second, and EV-LOG-002 documents a ten‑fold outbound rate increase. Metrics EV-MET-001 confirm outbound calls spiking to 525 req/s, matching the code‑driven behavior.
falsification_criteria: Runtime inspection shows MAX_RETRIES remained at 2 during the incident
Configuration variable BACKOFF_SECONDS is non‑zero in the deployed container
No more than two retry attempts are observed for any request in tracing data
verification_plan: Retrieve the deployed container image hash and compare its source to the commit containing EV-CODE-002
Query the environment variables of the running service for BACKOFF_SECONDS and MAX_RETRIES values at the incident timestamp
Instrument the retry loop to log the attempt count per request and verify counts exceed two
Cross‑reference retry timestamps with the code version to ensure the new logic was active

hypotheses.claim: The downstream payment gateway’s rate‑limiting (HTTP 429) and service‑unavailable responses (HTTP 503) triggered the client’s retry loop, and the gateway’s capacity limits amplified the stampede independently of client configuration.
hypotheses.supporting_reasoning: EV-LOG-003 records the initial 503 response that started the retry process. EV-LOG-001 notes the gateway collapsing under the retry surge, with both 429 and 503 responses. Metrics EV-MET-002 and EV-MET-003 show spikes to 75 % and 48 % respectively for those error codes, and EV-MET-007 reports a strong correlation (0.82) between outbound calls and 429 rate, indicating the gateway’s feedback loop drove the storm.
falsification_criteria: Gateway logs for the interval show no 429 or 503 responses
Rate‑limit thresholds were not reached according to gateway monitoring
Outbound request volume does not correlate with gateway error responses
verification_plan: Obtain the downstream gateway’s access logs for the incident window and count 503 and 429 status codes
Review the gateway’s rate‑limit configuration and compare request volume against thresholds
Plot outbound request timestamps against gateway error timestamps to assess temporal correlation
Check whether the gateway reported resource exhaustion or throttling events during the period

hypotheses.claim: The surge was caused by synchronized, jitter‑free retries due to the zero back‑off setting, not by increased inbound traffic, as evidenced by the drop in ingress rate concurrent with the outbound spike.
hypotheses.supporting_reasoning: EV-MET-004 shows ingress requests fell to 48 req/s while EV-MET-001 records outbound calls jumping to 525 req/s, indicating traffic was generated internally. The code change in EV-CODE-002 (and matching config EV-CODE-006) removed any back‑off delay, eliminating jitter and causing many instances to retry at the same moment, which aligns with the high correlation reported in EV-MET-007.
falsification_criteria: Back‑off value was non‑zero at runtime, introducing jitter
Ingress request rate was actually higher than baseline during the incident
Outbound spikes occur without any change to back‑off configuration
verification_plan: Inspect the live configuration of BACKOFF_SECONDS in the running containers
Analyze timestamps of retry attempts across multiple service instances to detect synchronization
Compare ingress request metrics before, during, and after the incident to confirm the drop
Run a controlled test with back‑off enabled to verify reduction in outbound spike
